stem: Describe Garibaldi's campaign in Sicily and southern Italy in 1860.

points.description: Sailed with the Thousand from near Genoa; landed at Marsala (May 1860) to support a Sicilian rising.
Won at Calatafimi and took Palermo; ruled Sicily as dictator in Victor Emmanuel's name.
Crossed to the mainland (August) and entered Naples (7 September).
Won the battle of the Volturno (October); plebiscites; handed over at Teano.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Garibaldi sailed with about a thousand volunteers from near Genoa and landed at Marsala in May 1860 to support a rising in Sicily. He won at Calatafimi, captured Palermo and ruled Sicily as dictator in the name of Victor Emmanuel. In August he crossed to the mainland, the Bourbon army collapsed, and he entered Naples on 7 September. He defeated the Bourbon forces on the Volturno in October, and after plebiscites he handed the south to the king at Teano.

stem: Explain why Cavour was worried by Garibaldi's success in 1860.

points.description: Identifies fear that Garibaldi would attack Rome.
Explains that Rome was protected by French troops, so this risked war with France (and Austria).
Identifies fear that the democrats/republicans would control the south.
Explains that this could challenge the king's leadership / Cavour's moderate Italy.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Cavour feared that Garibaldi, after taking Naples, would march on Rome. Rome was protected by French troops, so an attack could bring war with France, Piedmont's ally, and perhaps Austria as well. He also feared that Garibaldi and the democrats would control the south and set up a government that challenged the king, threatening the moderate, monarchist Italy that Cavour wanted.

hints: Think about France and about who would rule the south.

stem: Explain why other European countries were important to the completion of Italian unification between 1860 and 1870.

points.description: Identifies Prussia's role in 1866.
Explains that Prussia's victory at Königgrätz, not Italian arms, won Venetia.
Identifies France's role over Rome.
Explains that French troops protected the pope (Mentana 1867) until withdrawn in 1870 during the Franco-Prussian War.
Identifies Britain's / France's acceptance of change in 1860.
Explains that Britain supported Italians' right to choose and did not interfere with Garibaldi; Napoleon accepted the invasion of the Papal States.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Prussia was decisive in 1866: Italy was defeated at Custoza and Lissa, but Prussia's victory over Austria at Königgrätz forced Austria to give up Venetia. France blocked the way to Rome: its troops protected the pope and defeated Garibaldi at Mentana in 1867, and Rome could only be taken in 1870 when France withdrew its garrison to fight Prussia. Britain also helped in 1860 by supporting the Italians' right to choose their own government and not interfering with Garibaldi, while Napoleon III accepted Piedmont's invasion of the Papal States.

hints: Consider each of Prussia, France and Britain.

stem:
Study the sources and answer the questions.

**Source A** — a memoir by a fictional volunteer of the Thousand, written in 1890 (invented for this question)

> We were students, workers and adventurers, armed with old muskets. At Calatafimi the enemy held the hill and we had no right to win. But the General walked up the slope as if on parade, and we followed him. He did not ask for anything for himself. Italy was made by men who believed in him.

**Source B** — an article by a fictional Piedmontese official in a Turin journal, written in 1861 (invented for this question)

> The romantic tale of the Thousand should not blind us. The Bourbon army was rotten before a single shot was fired. Without the King's regiments, which secured the Marches and Umbria and kept the French from interfering, Garibaldi's conquests would have ended in disaster or in war with France.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Source A is by a volunteer who fought at Calatafimi, so he saw events at first hand, but he wrote thirty years later in a memoir full of admiration, so his memory may be coloured by legend. Some details are confirmed: Calatafimi was a hard-won victory against a strong position, and Garibaldi did refuse rewards. Source B was written in 1861 by a Piedmontese official, whose state wanted the credit for unification to go to the king; it plays down Garibaldi's victories and ignores the Sicilian rising. Yet its main points are also confirmed: the Bourbon army was poorly led, and the king's army did occupy the Marches and Umbria. Both are one-sided, but B is slightly more reliable for the wider events because its claims can be checked, while A is more useful for the spirit of the volunteers.

parts.explanation: Reliability judged from provenance and from content checked against own knowledge.

hints: Each writer has a reason to give credit to a different person or institution.

Important: inspired support; defence of Rome 1849; volunteers in 1859.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Garibaldi made a vital contribution. In 1860 he conquered Sicily and Naples with a small volunteer force, something no one else attempted, and at Teano he handed them to Victor Emmanuel, turning Cavour's northern kingdom into the Kingdom of Italy. His defence of Rome in 1849 and his fame made him a symbol that won support for unification in Italy and abroad.

However, his success depended on others. The Sicilians had already risen, the Bourbon army was poorly led, and Cavour allowed the expedition to sail. It was the Piedmontese army that occupied the Marches and Umbria and made sure the south joined the kingdom. After 1861 Garibaldi's own attempts to take Rome failed at Aspromonte and Mentana; Venetia was won in 1866 and Rome in 1870 because Prussia defeated Austria and France.

Overall Garibaldi was essential to the events of 1860, and without him the south might not have joined Italy for many years, but unification as a whole depended more on Piedmont's state and on the wars of other powers.

parts.explanation: Both sides and a supported judgement for the top level.

hints: In (b), compare Garibaldi with Cavour, Victor Emmanuel and foreign powers, and treat 1860 and 1866-70 separately.
